D2-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative
On-Policy Distillation

Bowen Fang ††thanks: This work was done during an internship at Amazon. Affiliation: Columbia University Email: bf2504@columbia.edu    Dingmin Wang Affiliation: AWS AI Lab Email: wdimmy@amazon.com    Hengzhi Pei Affiliation: Amazon AGI Email: philepei@amazon.com
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher’s next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher’s log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher’s shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose D2-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target’s distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, D2-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses: the student generates a response and, at each prefix it visits, learns from the teacher’s next-token distribution (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Training on student-generated prefixes reduces the mismatch between the responses seen in training and those the student generates at inference (Ross et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020). Prior work has studied several aspects of on-policy distillation, including the efficient use of student-generated responses (Ko et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2025), teacher entropy (Jin et al., 2026), teacher–student disagreement (Xing et al., 2026), and training stability (Xie et al., 2026). These studies show that the way teacher supervision is constructed and transferred matters beyond the choice of teacher alone.

However, the teacher’s distribution may not be the best target: prior work shows that a more capable teacher does not necessarily yield a better student (Mirzadeh et al., 2020; Li et al., 2026). Extrapolative OPD aims to construct a better target beyond the teacher by amplifying the teacher’s log-probability shift from a reference policy. If the teacher was obtained from the reference by KL-regularized post-training, this shift equals its regularized QQ-function up to scale and a prefix-dependent constant (Geist et al., 2019; Rafailov et al., 2024), so amplifying it moves probability toward tokens with higher teacher QQ-values. Constructing an extrapolative target involves two decisions: the direction in which the target moves away from the teacher, and the distance it moves. In existing methods, the distance is tied to the direction. For example, ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026) fixes the direction through its reference, but under a fixed coefficient its distance varies with the scale of the teacher–reference gap across prefixes; in Direct-OPD (Feng et al., 2026), changing the batch-shared adaptive coefficient generally changes both the direction and the distance. In both cases, the distance follows from the coefficient and the log-ratios at each prefix, rather than from how far the target can be trusted beyond the teacher. We show that, under fixed-coefficient extrapolation, the target can place substantial probability on tokens the teacher rarely predicts, even when the error in the extrapolation signal is small on average under the teacher.

To address this coupling, we propose D2-OPD, which decouples distance from direction. First, a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target’s distance from the teacher, independently of the scale of the extrapolation signal; this also bounds the probability the target can assign to tokens the teacher rarely predicts. Second, we construct the direction by combining the teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap. The weights adapt at each prefix, giving more weight to the nearer signal. Finally, forward KL transfers the target while maintaining non-vanishing gradients for tokens rarely generated by the student.

We evaluate D2-OPD on three Qwen3 teacher–student pairs covering a setting where standard OPD performs well, a setting for which prior work recommends a supervised cold start (Li et al., 2026), and a setting without a separate teacher reference. D2-OPD achieves the highest average score across AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23 in all three settings. In Qwen3-8B →\rightarrow Qwen3-4B-Base distillation, it outperforms OPD by 19.62 points and the strongest baseline by 9.45 points. In the cold-start setting, it exceeds the released SFT + OPD recipe without supervised fine-tuning. Ablations confirm the contributions of the distance constraint, the combined direction, and forward-KL distillation. Response-length and entropy analyses indicate that the gains are not merely due to longer answers or more concentrated student policies.

2 Related work

Distillation objectives.

Knowledge distillation trains students using teacher predictions, with applications to policy learning and reasoning (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016; Rusu et al., 2016; Teh et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2018; Hsieh et al., 2023; Shridhar et al., 2023). On-policy imitation and distillation reduce the mismatch between training and inference by training on the learner’s own trajectories (Ross et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2024). Related work studies divergence choices and response reuse for transferring teacher supervision (Wen et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2025).

Teacher–student gaps.

A larger or more capable teacher does not necessarily produce a better student (Mirzadeh et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2024; Shing et al., 2025; Furlanello et al., 2018; Burns et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). EOPD (Jin et al., 2026) adds forward KL when teacher entropy is high, while TrOPD (Xing et al., 2026) applies forward KL where teacher–student disagreement is large. Li et al. (2026) link training failure to low initial overlap between the teacher’s and student’s high-probability token sets.

Extrapolation and distance constraints.

Under KL-regularized optimization, the log-ratio between the optimized policy and its reference encodes the regularized QQ-function (Ouyang et al., 2022; Geist et al., 2019; Rafailov et al., 2023; Rafailov et al., 2024). Extrapolative methods use this relation to construct new distillation targets. ExOPD uses a fixed coefficient to scale a direction set by its reference (Yang et al., 2026). Direct-OPD transfers the teacher’s post-training shift through an objective anchored at the initial student, with an adaptive regularization coefficient applied uniformly across the batch (Feng et al., 2026). Changing this coefficient generally changes both the target’s direction and its distance relative to the teacher. TOP-D constructs a proximal teacher and uses trust-region updates (Xie et al., 2026); ERPD constrains distillation relative to the rollout policy (Chen et al., 2026).

3 Preliminaries

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the training prompt distribution and πθ\pi_{\theta} the current student with parameters θ\theta. For a prompt x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, we sample GG responses y1,…,yGy_{1},\ldots,y_{G} from the student. The index ii identifies a response, tt a token position, and |yi||y_{i}| its response length. Writing yi,<ty_{i,<t} for the tokens before position tt, we define the prefix hi,t=(x,yi,<t)h_{i,t}=(x,y_{i,<t}). We use yy, hh, and aa for a generic response, prefix, and candidate next token. We denote the initial student by π0\pi_{0}, the post-trained teacher by q+q^{+}, and the checkpoint from which the teacher was post-trained by treft_{\mathrm{ref}}. For any policy π\pi, π⁡(a∣h)\pi(a\mid h) denotes a token probability and π(⋅∣h)\pi(\cdot\mid h) the next-token distribution, while π⁡(y∣x)\pi(y\mid x) denotes a response probability. Let KK be the number of candidate tokens and S⁡(h)S(h) the top-KK tokens under the teacher distribution q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h). For any token set BB, write π⁡(B∣h)=∑a∈Bπ⁡(a∣h)\pi(B\mid h)=\sum_{a\in B}\pi(a\mid h). The distribution renormalized on S⁡(h)S(h) is πS​(a∣h)=π⁡(a∣h)/π⁡(S⁡(h)∣h)\pi_{S}(a\mid h)=\pi(a\mid h)/\pi(S(h)\mid h) for a∈S⁡(h)a\in S(h), and zero otherwise. In particular, qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h) and πθ,S(⋅∣h)\pi_{\theta,S}(\cdot\mid h) denote the renormalized teacher and student distributions, respectively, renormalized over the same top-KK token set S⁡(h)S(h).

3.1 On-policy distillation

Reverse-KL OPD (Gu et al., 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025) minimizes the loss ℒOPD​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta),

ℒOPD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟[DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥q+(⋅∣x))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,q^{+}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right]. (1)

At a student-generated prefix, the token reward is rθ​(h,a)=log⁡(q+​(a∣h)/πθ​(a∣h))r_{\theta}(h,a)=\log(q^{+}(a\mid h)/\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h)). Its expectation under the student is the negative reverse KL:

𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣h)[rθ(h,a)]=−DKL(πθ(⋅∣h)∥q+(⋅∣h)).\underset{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)}{\mathbb{E}}[r_{\theta}(h,a)]=-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)\|q^{+}(\cdot\mid h)).

Maximizing the expected sum of token rewards is equivalent to minimizing Eq. (1).

3.2 Extrapolative targets

For a reference bb, OPD is KL-regularized RL with reward log⁡(q+​(y∣x)/b⁡(y∣x))\log(q^{+}(y\mid x)/b(y\mid x)) and regularizer anchored at b(⋅∣x)b(\cdot\mid x). Scaling that reward by λ>0\lambda>0 gives the ExOPD target πλ⋆\pi^{\star}_{\lambda} (Yang et al., 2026),

πλ⋆​(y∣x)∝b⁡(y∣x)​(q+​(y∣x)b⁡(y∣x))λ.\pi^{\star}_{\lambda}(y\mid x)\propto b(y\mid x)\left(\frac{q^{+}(y\mid x)}{b(y\mid x)}\right)^{\lambda}. (2)

It recovers the teacher at λ=1\lambda=1 and extrapolates along log⁡(q+​(y∣x)/b⁡(y∣x))\log(q^{+}(y\mid x)/b(y\mid x)) for λ>1\lambda>1.

The teacher reference gives this direction a policy-improvement interpretation. Let ΔT​(h,a)=log⁡(q+​(a∣h)/tref​(a∣h))\Delta_{T}(h,a)=\log(q^{+}(a\mid h)/t_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid h)) be the teacher’s post-training shift. If q+q^{+} solves a KL-regularized objective relative to treft_{\mathrm{ref}} with coefficient βT>0\beta_{T}>0, its regularized QQ-function Q+​(h,a)Q^{+}(h,a) satisfies the following identity for an action-independent term c⁡(h)c(h) (Geist et al., 2019; Rafailov et al., 2024):

βT​ΔT​(h,a)=Q+​(h,a)−c⁡(h).\beta_{T}\Delta_{T}(h,a)=Q^{+}(h,a)-c(h). (3)

ΔT​(h,a)\Delta_{T}(h,a) and Q+​(h,a)Q^{+}(h,a) rank tokens identically. The teacher’s post-training shift can therefore serve as a signal for further policy improvement. Direct-OPD uses ΔT​(h,a)\Delta_{T}(h,a) as its token reward and anchors its regularizer at π0\pi_{0}, with regularization coefficient α>0\alpha>0. Its optimal target π⋆\pi^{\star} is (Feng et al., 2026)

π⋆​(y∣x)∝π0​(y∣x)​(q+​(y∣x)tref​(y∣x))1/α.\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{0}(y\mid x)\left(\frac{q^{+}(y\mid x)}{t_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}\right)^{1/\alpha}. (4)

This target need not lie on the teacher-reference ray in Eq. (2). In both objectives, distance from q+(⋅∣x)q^{+}(\cdot\mid x) depends on the log-ratio scale as well as the coefficient. Appendix G gives the full objectives.

4 Method

The objectives in Section 3.2 tie two decisions together: the direction in which the target leaves the teacher, and how far it travels. We construct the extrapolation direction and separately bound the target’s distance from the teacher at each prefix.

For a prefix hh visited by a student rollout, we build a target distribution q~(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h) along a direction derived from two reference signals, at a distance we bound explicitly, and train the student toward it with forward KL, using the loss ℒ⁡(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta):

ℒ(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟{yi}i=1G∼πθ(⋅∣x)[1∑i=1G|yi|∑i=1G∑t=1|yi|DKL(q~(⋅∣hi,t)∥πθ(⋅∣hi,t))].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{D}\\ \{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\Biggl[\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}|y_{i}|}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h_{i,t})\,\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{i,t})\right)\Biggr].

 (5)

We next explain the rationales behind each of our design choices. Section 4.1 bounds how far q~(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h) may move from the teacher, through a hard radius ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 and a soft coefficient 0<κ≤10<\kappa\leq 1. Section 4.2 determines the combined direction dη​(h,a)d_{\eta}(h,a), where η⁡(h)∈[0,1]\eta(h)\in[0,1] is derived to weight the student signal by minimizing relative deviation from both signals. Section 4.3 explains why the divergence in Eq. (5) is forward rather than reverse KL.

4.1 Limiting the extrapolation distance

As discussed in Section 3.2, existing extrapolation coefficients control the distance from q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h) only indirectly: a coefficient multiplies a log-ratio whose scale varies across prefixes, so one value can hold the target close to q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h) at one prefix and carry it much farther at another. The distance is worth controlling on its own, because the teacher is a policy we can observe and evaluate, whereas a target farther from q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h) rests more heavily on extrapolation. For a candidate target distribution q(⋅∣h)q(\cdot\mid h) supported on S⁡(h)S(h), let 𝒦(q;h)=DKL(q(⋅∣h)∥qS+(⋅∣h))\mathcal{K}(q;h)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(\cdot\mid h)\|q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)). We impose 𝒦⁡(q,h)≤ϵ\mathcal{K}(q;h)\leq\epsilon at every prefix, which bounds how far the target may move. To express token preference in the target distribution, let d⁡(h,a)d(h,a) be a per-token score function on S⁡(h)S(h), whose construction is introduced in Section 4.2. We choose q~(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h) to increase the expected value of d⁡(h,a)d(h,a) while penalizing its KL distance from the renormalized teacher qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h). The coefficient κ\kappa controls this trade-off, and the constraint limits the distance to ϵ\epsilon. Therefore, the target distribution q~(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h) is defined as:

q~(⋅∣h)=arg​maxq(⋅∣h)\displaystyle\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)=\argmax_{q(\cdot\mid h)} (1−κ)​𝔼a∼q(⋅∣h)​[d⁡(h,a)]\displaystyle(1-\kappa)\underset{a\sim q(\cdot\mid h)}{\mathbb{E}}[d(h,a)] (6)
−κ​𝒦​(q,h)\displaystyle-\kappa\mathcal{K}(q;h)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} 𝒦⁡(q,h)≤ϵ.\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(q;h)\leq\epsilon.

Solving the constrained problem.

Let λ⁡(h)≥0\lambda(h)\geq 0 be the Lagrange multiplier on the KL constraint and β⁡(h)\beta(h) the extrapolation coefficient. The optimum of Eq. (6) has the form

q~​(a∣h)\displaystyle\tilde{q}(a\mid h) ∝qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[β⁡(h)​d​(h,a)],\displaystyle\propto q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp\!\left[\beta(h)d(h,a)\right], (7)
β⁡(h)\displaystyle\beta(h) =1−κκ+λ⁡(h).\displaystyle=\frac{1-\kappa}{\kappa+\lambda(h)}.

The target is normalized over S⁡(h)S(h) and zero elsewhere. The unconstrained solution yields λ⁡(h)=0\lambda(h)=0 and coefficient βmax=(1−κ)/κ\beta_{\max}=(1-\kappa)/\kappa. At κ=1\kappa=1, the target reduces to qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h) while smaller values allow stronger extrapolation.

For 0<κ<10<\kappa<1, we retain the unconstrained target if it satisfies the bound; otherwise, we perform 24 bisection iterations on [0,βmax][0,\beta_{\max}], where DKL(q~(⋅∣h)∥qS+(⋅∣h))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)\|q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)) is nondecreasing in β⁡(h)\beta(h), to find the constraint boundary. We process prefixes in parallel on the teacher’s top-KK support. The search is computationally inexpensive.11 1 On a single A100 40GB GPU, the search takes about 7.2 ms for 32,768 prefixes, equivalent to eight responses of 4,096 tokens each, with K=16K=16 in FP32. Including direction construction takes about 9.3 ms.

ExOPD observes longer responses under stronger extrapolation and attributes this partly to potential length bias in the implicit reward (Yang et al., 2026). We propose another possible mechanism: extrapolation may amplify overestimated scores for low-probability teacher tokens, potentially encouraging repetitive or prolonged reasoning. The KL bound limits the probability mass assigned to such tokens.

Proposition 1

At a fixed prefix hh, let B⊆S⁡(h)B\subseteq S(h) be a set of tokens with renormalized teacher probability ρ⁡(h)=qS+​(B∣h)\rho(h)=q_{S}^{+}(B\mid h), where 0<ρ⁡(h)<10<\rho(h)<1. Every target q(⋅∣h)q(\cdot\mid h) satisfying 𝒦⁡(q,h)≤ϵ\mathcal{K}(q;h)\leq\epsilon obeys

q⁡(B∣h)≤ϵ+log⁡2log⁡(1/ρ⁡(h)).q(B\mid h)\leq\frac{\epsilon+\log 2}{\log(1/\rho(h))}. (8)

For fixed ϵ\epsilon, this bound tends to zero as the teacher probability ρ⁡(h)\rho(h) tends to zero. Appendix H contains the proof and expands on the connection to response-length growth. It also shows that fixed-coefficient extrapolation can assign substantial probability to these tokens even when the score error is small in teacher-weighted mean square.

4.2 Determining the extrapolation direction

The teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap typically point in different directions. Although both provide useful guidance, constructing a target requires combining them into a single direction. As shown in Section 3.2, Direct-OPD’s regularization coefficient α\alpha controls both direction and distance, without a separate criterion for combining the signals. We therefore introduce an explicit criterion that balances the direction’s relative deviation from the two signals.

We use the teacher-reference signal ΔT​(h,a)=log⁡(q+​(a∣h)/tref​(a∣h))\Delta_{T}(h,a)=\log(q^{+}(a\mid h)/t_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid h)) and the student signal Δπ0​(h,a)=log⁡(q+​(a∣h)/π0​(a∣h))\Delta_{\pi_{0}}(h,a)=\log(q^{+}(a\mid h)/\pi_{0}(a\mid h)). For convenience, we center both signals so that their variances equal their squared norms under qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h). At each prefix, for j∈{T,π0}j\in\{T,\pi_{0}\}, we define Δjc(h,a)=Δj(h,a)−𝔼b∼qS+(⋅∣h)[Δj(h,b)]\Delta_{j}^{c}(h,a)=\Delta_{j}(h,a)-\mathbb{E}_{b\sim q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)}[\Delta_{j}(h,b)].

Let σT2​(h)\sigma_{T}^{2}(h) and σπ2​(h)\sigma_{\pi}^{2}(h) denote the variances of the teacher-reference and student signals, respectively, under qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h). In centered log-probability space weighted by qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h), each signal’s variance is the squared distance from the teacher to its reference. We refer to σT​(h)\sigma_{T}(h) and σπ​(h)\sigma_{\pi}(h) as reference distances and normalize each squared deviation by its corresponding squared reference distance. When both reference distances are positive, let ℛT(d;h)=𝔼a∼qS+(⋅∣h)[(d(h,a)−ΔTc(h,a))2]/σT2(h)\mathcal{R}_{T}(d;h)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)}[(d(h,a)-\Delta_{T}^{c}(h,a))^{2}]/\sigma_{T}^{2}(h) and define ℛπ​(d,h)\mathcal{R}_{\pi}(d;h) analogously using Δπ0c​(h,a)\Delta_{\pi_{0}}^{c}(h,a) and σπ2​(h)\sigma_{\pi}^{2}(h). We define dη​(h,⋅)d_{\eta}(h,\cdot) as:

dη​(h,⋅)=arg​mind⁡(h,⋅)\displaystyle d_{\eta}(h,\cdot)=\argmin_{d(h,\cdot)} ℛT​(d,h)+ℛπ​(d,h)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{T}(d;h)+\mathcal{R}_{\pi}(d;h) (9)

When both reference distances σT​(h)\sigma_{T}(h) and σπ​(h)\sigma_{\pi}(h) are positive, the objective above has the unique minimizer

The proof is given in Appendix H. The weight η⁡(h)\eta(h) is determined by the two signals at each prefix, giving more weight to the nearer reference.

dη​(h,a)∝σπ​(h)​u​(h,a)+σT​(h)​v​(h,a).d_{\eta}(h,a)\propto\sigma_{\pi}(h)u(h,a)+\sigma_{T}(h)v(h,a). (11)

Figure 2 illustrates how this combination places the direction closer to that of the nearer reference.

In our implementation, we compute the closed-form solution directly without forming u⁡(h,a)u(h,a) and v⁡(h,a)v(h,a), avoiding division by either reference distance. We use Eq. (10) when both reference distances exceed 10−310^{-3}. If only one is at most 10−310^{-3}, we omit that signal and use the other centered signal. tη​(a∣h)∝qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[−dη​(h,a)].t_{\eta}(a\mid h)\propto q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp[-d_{\eta}(h,a)]. (12)

After normalization over S⁡(h)S(h), log⁡(qS+​(a∣h)/tη​(a∣h))\log(q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)/t_{\eta}(a\mid h)) equals dη​(h,a)d_{\eta}(h,a) up to a token-independent constant. This constructed reference requires no additional model.

4.3 Transferring the target to the student

The constructed target can place probability to tokens that are rare under the student. We use forward KL because its gradient remains non-vanishing in this case. The forward-KL gradient with respect to the student logit is πθ​(a∣h)−q~​(a∣h)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h)-\tilde{q}(a\mid h). For tokens with positive target probability, it approaches −q~​(a∣h)-\tilde{q}(a\mid h) as πθ​(a∣h)→0\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h)\to 0, whereas the reverse-KL gradient vanishes.

In practice, S⁡(h)S(h) contains the top-KK tokens under the teacher distribution q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h). We construct and renormalize q~(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h) on S⁡(h)S(h), but keep the student distribution over the full vocabulary. Estimating forward KL from student-sampled tokens can have high variance. The importance weights q~​(a∣h)/πθ​(a∣h)\tilde{q}(a\mid h)/\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h) can be large when the target assigns substantial probability to tokens the student rarely samples. We therefore compute the exact sum over all tokens in S⁡(h)S(h) at each visited prefix. With support mass πθ​(S​(h)∣h)\pi_{\theta}(S(h)\mid h) and renormalized student πθ,S(⋅∣h)\pi_{\theta,S}(\cdot\mid h) defined in Section 3, we have

DKL(q~(⋅∣h)∥πθ(⋅∣h))=−logπθ(S(h)∣h)+DKL(q~(⋅∣h)∥πθ,S(⋅∣h)).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h))=\\ &-\log\pi_{\theta}(S(h)\mid h)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)\|\pi_{\theta,S}(\cdot\mid h)).\end{aligned}

 (13)

The first term shifts student probability mass onto S⁡(h)S(h), while the second matches its relative distribution within it. Renormalizing the student removes the first term and its mass-transfer effect. Unlike Eq. (13), reverse KL has no such mass-transfer term and only adjusts relative probabilities within S⁡(h)S(h). We examine the importance of this forward-KL choice in the ablation experiments in Section 5.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental setup

Models.

We evaluate three teacher–student pairs covering three complementary settings. All models are from the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025). (1) Setting A distills Qwen3-8B into Qwen3-4B-Base, with tref=t_{\mathrm{ref}}= Qwen3-8B-Base. Under this setting, standard OPD performs well and a genuine teacher reference is available. (2) Setting B distills Qwen3-4B (non-thinking) into Qwen3-1.7B-Base, with tref=t_{\mathrm{ref}}= Qwen3-4B-Base. Li et al. (2026) report that OPD leads to poor performance under this setting and recommend a supervised finetuning as a cold start, while a genuine teacher reference is available. (3) Setting C distills Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 into Qwen3-8B-Base. Standard OPD performs well in this setting, but no teacher reference checkpoint is available, so we set tref=π0t_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{0}. There is then only one extrapolative direction, leaving ϵ\epsilon and κ\kappa as the active controls.

Training data.

Settings A and C train on the full DAPO-Math-17K dataset (Yu et al., 2025). Setting B trains on approximately 30K prompts from the math-domain subset of OpenThoughts3-1.2M (Guha et al., 2026). Every run trains for one epoch.

Evaluation.

We evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23 (Mathematical Association of America, n.d.a, n.d.b), reporting avg@16 with a shared maximum evaluation response length of 31,744 tokens. We report results from the final checkpoint of one training run per configuration.

Baselines.

We compare against OPD (Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), EOPD (Jin et al., 2026), TOP-D (Xie et al., 2026), ExOPD (Yang et al., 2026), and Direct-OPD (Feng et al., 2026). We use the on-policy variant of TOP-D, the reward-correction variant of ExOPD, and the published adaptive α\alpha controller of Direct-OPD. For method-specific hyperparameters, we use the authors’ recommended values. Appendix B gives implementation details and parameter-search results.

Hyperparameters.

All methods share the default training setup of Li et al. (2026), except for a maximum training response length of 4,096 tokens. Appendix A provides training and evaluation details.

Method parameters.

Unless otherwise stated, we use κ=0.05\kappa=0.05, with ϵ=1\epsilon=1 in Settings A and B and ϵ=4\epsilon=4 in Setting C. Appendix C describes parameter selection and sensitivity.

5.2 Main results

Tables 1–3 report the main results across the three settings. In these three tables, Avg is the mean score across the three benchmarks, and Δ\Delta denotes its difference from OPD. Bold and underline indicate the best and second-best results, respectively, among trained methods.

Setting A.

OPD improves the initial student’s average score from 19.58 to 27.57. Our method reaches 47.19, improving OPD by 19.62 points and the strongest baseline, TOP-D, by 9.45 points. It leads on all three benchmarks.

Setting B.

We also compare the SFT checkpoint and SFT + OPD recipe released by Li et al. (2026).

OPD w. forward KL uses Section 4.3 without extrapolation or direction selection. Forward KL alone raises OPD’s average score from 14.22 to 18.85. The full method reaches 22.31, exceeding ExOPD by 2.29 points and SFT + OPD by 1.51 points, without a supervised cold start. SFT + OPD remains stronger on AIME24 and AIME25; our method leads on AMC23.

Setting C.

We set tref=π0t_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{0} in ExOPD, Direct-OPD, and our method. Their reference directions coincide, so this setting isolates control along a fixed direction. The constraint binds more often here; we use ϵ=4\epsilon=4 (Appendix C). Our method reaches 46.27, improving OPD by 7.36 points and the strongest baseline, Direct-OPD, by 1.76 points. TOP-D, which constructs an intermediate teacher from the current student, also remains competitive.

Our method has the highest average score in all three settings, while the strongest competing baseline changes across settings.

5.3 Analysis

How restrictive is ϵ\epsilon?

To start with, we give a simple interpretation of the scale of ϵ\epsilon. For a one-hot target δa(⋅∣h)\delta_{a}(\cdot\mid h) that assigns all probability to a token a∈S⁡(h)a\in S(h), DKL(δa(⋅∣h)∥qS+(⋅∣h))=−logqS+(a∣h)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\delta_{a}(\cdot\mid h)\|q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h))=-\log q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h), which means that ϵ=1\epsilon=1 permits the target to concentrate entirely on a token with qS+​(a∣h)≥e−1≈0.37q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\geq e^{-1}\approx 0.37. Although this makes ϵ=1\epsilon=1 fairly permissive, Figure 5 shows that it still binds a meaningful fraction of positions in practice. The constraint binds on more than 60% of positions early in training and has a median active fraction of 34% over the second half of training. As expected, increasing κ\kappa makes the constraint less active, since the soft objective itself proposes less aggressive extrapolation. Even at κ=0.3\kappa=0.3, the hard constraint still binds on about 11% of positions.

Are the gains explained by longer responses?

ExOPD observes that extrapolation can increase response length (Yang et al., 2026). We observe the same behavior for ExOPD, but not for extrapolative methods in general. In Figure 3, D2-OPD and Direct-OPD remain among the shorter methods across all three settings. TOP-D has a similar length and also remains well below the generation limit. In contrast, ExOPD and EOPD generally produce much longer responses. It is the most obvious in Settings B and C, where several methods nearly exhaust the 31,744-token budget while D2-OPD does not.22 2 Our evaluation length limit matches the limit used by Li et al. (2026); Feng et al. (2026) and is larger than those used by Jin et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2026); Xie et al. (2026). D2-OPD achieves the highest average score in all three settings while generating shorter responses than several baselines.

Are the gains explained by lower entropy?

A common intuition is that a lower-entropy policy is more concentrated and may therefore achieve higher single-response accuracy (pass@1). Figure 4 shows that this does not explain our results. Across all three settings, D2-OPD remains among the higher-entropy students while achieving the best average score. TOP-D and Direct-OPD, which are also among the stronger baselines, generally lie in the higher-entropy group as well. Appendix E.2 examines the student–teacher entropy gap.

Computational cost.

Table 4 reports time and throughput per training step excluding rollout generation. D2-OPD has roughly comparable training cost to OPD, taking 15% more time per step. Appendix F describes this experiment’s setup.

5.4 Ablations

We conduct ablations in Setting A while keeping all other training and evaluation settings fixed. Each block in Table 5 removes or replaces one component of the full method: distance control, direction construction, the distillation loss, or extrapolation.

Disabling extrapolation causes the largest drop, reducing the average score from 47.19 to 34.22. With extrapolation retained, removing the hard distance constraint lowers the score to 43.30, while removing only the soft penalty gives 45.59. Thus, the hard bound contributes beyond the soft penalty.

Using only the student reference or teacher reference gives 45.12 and 44.27, respectively, whereas combining the signals performs better. Replacing forward KL with reverse KL lowers the score to 44.36. Retaining the support-mass term improves this to 45.36, still below the full method. This suggests that forward KL contributes beyond moving probability onto the candidate support.

6 Conclusion

We presented D2-OPD, decoupling extrapolation direction from distance in extrapolative on-policy distillation. The method combines two directional signals while enforcing a per-prefix KL bound on the target’s distance from the teacher. On three teacher–student settings, D2-OPD outperforms OPD baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Ablations show that combined direction signals, the distance constraint, and forward-KL distillation each contribute to these gains.

Limitations

Our experiments cover three teacher–student pairs from the Qwen3 family and three mathematical-reasoning benchmarks. They do not establish whether the same gains hold for other model families or tasks. The direction construction uses a teacher reference checkpoint when one is available. Without that checkpoint, the two directions coincide, so the method cannot use the teacher’s post-training shift as a separate signal. The distance bound and soft extrapolation coefficient are hyperparameters; the method does not determine an optimal extrapolation distance. The parameter study also shows that the choice of distance bound matters across settings.

Ethical Considerations

Distillation can transfer undesirable behavior from the teacher, including biased or harmful outputs. Our mathematical-reasoning evaluations do not assess these behaviors or privacy risks. Training and evaluation also incur energy costs.

Appendix A Training and evaluation details

Our experiments focus on mathematical reasoning, with evaluation on English-language competition problems. We do not assess performance across languages, specific linguistic phenomena, or demographic groups.

Training.

All methods share the same default training setup of Li et al. (2026), except that we set the maximum response length to 4,096 rather than 7,168 tokens. This lies between the 3K and 7K moderate lengths that they report as yielding the strongest results (Li et al., 2026). Table 6 lists the default training hyperparameters.

Evaluation.

We report avg@16 using temperature 0.7, top-pp sampling with p=0.95p=0.95, and a maximum response length of 31,744 tokens. Responses are graded using the rule-based verifier of Sheng et al. (2025). Each setting is evaluated with the same template used during training.

Hardware and compute.

All methods were trained on AWS nodes with eight NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs per node. Settings A and B used one node, and Setting C used two nodes. Training for the reported experiments required approximately 9,000 GPU-hours across 50 runs: 33 in Setting A, eight in B, and nine in C. These runs cover the main comparisons, ablations, parameter sweeps, and constraint-activity analysis. The calculation uses approximate average training times of 20, 16, and 18 hours per run in Settings A, B, and C, respectively.

Appendix D Per-benchmark ablations

Table 10 gives the AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23 scores for the ablations summarized in Table 5.

Constraint variants.

The −κ-\kappa variant sets κ=0\kappa=0 and retains ϵ=1\epsilon=1. The −ϵ-\epsilon variant sets ϵ=106\epsilon=10^{6} to make the constraint slack and retains κ=0.05\kappa=0.05. The −-both variant uses κ=0\kappa=0 and ϵ=106\epsilon=10^{6}, with the extrapolation coefficient limited only by the numerical cap of 10410^{4}.

Direction variants.

The π0\pi_{0}-alone and treft_{\mathrm{ref}}-alone variants replace the combined score by Δπ0c​(h,a)\Delta_{\pi_{0}}^{c}(h,a) and ΔTc​(h,a)\Delta_{T}^{c}(h,a), respectively, while retaining ϵ=1\epsilon=1 and κ=0.05\kappa=0.05. If the selected signal’s reference distance is at most 10−310^{-3}, its score is set to zero.

KL and target variants.

Reverse KL uses DKL(πθ,S(⋅∣h)∥q~(⋅∣h))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta,S}(\cdot\mid h)\|\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)), with the student renormalized on S⁡(h)S(h). The variant with mass adds −log⁡πθ​(S⁡(h)∣h)-\log\pi_{\theta}(S(h)\mid h), retaining the support-mass term in Eq. (13). Both variants retain the full method’s target construction. The tilt-off variant uses the renormalized teacher distribution qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h) as the target and retains forward-KL distillation.

Appendix F Computational-cost experiment setup

We use the model checkpoints from Setting A on two NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs on one node. All methods process the same saved batch of 16 prompts with four responses per prompt. The maximum prompt and response lengths are 1,024 and 4,096 tokens, respectively.

Timing a full training step would include differences in the responses generated by each method. In particular, response length affects both generation and training time. Reusing the same saved responses fixes the token sequences and their lengths, allowing us to compare the cost of computing supervision and updating the student.

We discard the first two training steps as warm-up and report the mean time over the following three steps. The timed computation includes model scoring, target or reward construction, and student optimization. Throughput counts valid prompt and response tokens across both GPUs.

Appendix G Extrapolative distillation objectives

This appendix gives the baseline objectives summarized in Section 3.

ExOPD.

For an arbitrary reference bb, Yang et al. (2026) rewrite reverse-KL OPD as

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[logq+​(y∣x)b⁡(y∣x)\displaystyle\max_{\theta}\;\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{D}\\ y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\Bigl[\log\frac{q^{+}(y\mid x)}{b(y\mid x)} (14)
−DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥b(⋅∣x))].\displaystyle-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,b(\cdot\mid x)\right)\Bigr].

Scaling the reward by λ>0\lambda>0 gives Eq. (2). The target interpolates between b(⋅∣x)b(\cdot\mid x) and q+(⋅∣x)q^{+}(\cdot\mid x) for λ<1\lambda<1, recovers q+(⋅∣x)q^{+}(\cdot\mid x) at λ=1\lambda=1, and continues past it along log⁡(q+​(y∣x)/b⁡(y∣x))\log(q^{+}(y\mid x)/b(y\mid x)) for λ>1\lambda>1.

Direct-OPD.

Direct-OPD (Feng et al., 2026) transfers the teacher’s pre- to post-training log-ratio and regularizes the student toward its own initialization:

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[logq+​(y∣x)tref​(y∣x)\displaystyle\max_{\theta}\;\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{D}\\ y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\Bigl[\log\frac{q^{+}(y\mid x)}{t_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)} (15)
−αDKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x))].\displaystyle-\alpha D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\Bigr].

Its optimum is Eq. (4). Direct-OPD adapts a shared regularization coefficient using the batch’s mean teacher-shift reward. For the corresponding fixed-prefix objective, denote its target by qDirect(⋅∣h)q_{\mathrm{Direct}}(\cdot\mid h). It can be written relative to the teacher as

qDirect​(a∣h)∝π0​(a∣h)​exp⁡[ΔT​(h,a)/α]\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{Direct}}(a\mid h)\propto\pi_{0}(a\mid h)\exp[\Delta_{T}(h,a)/\alpha] (16)
=q+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[α−1​ΔT​(h,a)−Δπ0​(h,a)].\displaystyle=q^{+}(a\mid h)\exp\!\bigl[\alpha^{-1}\Delta_{T}(h,a)-\Delta_{\pi_{0}}(h,a)\bigr].

Changing α\alpha generally changes both direction and distance relative to q+(⋅∣h)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h). ExOPD with a fixed reference keeps the direction fixed, but the realized distance still depends on the scale of its log-ratio at each prefix. Our method constructs the direction first, then selects a separate coefficient at each prefix to enforce DKL(q~(⋅∣h)∥qS+(⋅∣h))≤ϵD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde{q}(\cdot\mid h)\|q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h))\leq\epsilon.

Appendix H Direction and distance in target construction

We provide proofs for Propositions 1 and 2, together with examples and further discussion of direction and distance in target construction. We fix a prefix hh and use the finite candidate support S⁡(h)S(h). The renormalized teacher qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h) is positive on this support, and candidate targets are zero outside it.

H.1 Distance

Proof of Proposition 1.

Let BB and ρ⁡(h)=qS+​(B∣h)\rho(h)=q_{S}^{+}(B\mid h) be as in the proposition. Let w⁡(h)=q⁡(B∣h)w(h)=q(B\mid h) and let Hbin​(w)=−w​log⁡w−(1−w)​log⁡(1−w)H_{\mathrm{bin}}(w)=-w\log w-(1-w)\log(1-w) denote binary entropy. Grouping tokens into BB and its complement gives

DKL(q(⋅∣h)∥qS+(⋅∣h))\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(\cdot\mid h)\|q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)) (17)
≥w⁡(h)​log​w⁡(h)ρ⁡(h)+(1−w⁡(h))​log​1−w⁡(h)1−ρ⁡(h)\displaystyle\geq w(h)\log\frac{w(h)}{\rho(h)}+(1-w(h))\log\frac{1-w(h)}{1-\rho(h)}
=w⁡(h)​log​1ρ⁡(h)+(1−w⁡(h))​log​11−ρ⁡(h)\displaystyle=w(h)\log\frac{1}{\rho(h)}+(1-w(h))\log\frac{1}{1-\rho(h)}
−Hbin​(w​(h))\displaystyle-H_{\mathrm{bin}}(w(h))
≥w⁡(h)​log⁡1ρ⁡(h)−log⁡2.\displaystyle\geq w(h)\log\frac{1}{\rho(h)}-\log 2.

Combining this inequality with the KL constraint proves the bound. □\square

Fixed-coefficient counterexample.

For every fixed extrapolation coefficient β>0\beta>0 and target mass m∈(0,1)m\in(0,1), there are centered score errors eρ​(h,a)e_{\rho}(h,a) with 𝔼a∼qS+(⋅∣h)[eρ(h,a)2]→0\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)}[e_{\rho}(h,a)^{2}]\to 0 such that the normalized target qβ​(a∣h)∝qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[β​eρ​(h,a)]q_{\beta}(a\mid h)\propto q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp[\beta e_{\rho}(h,a)] assigns probability mm to BB, even as ρ⁡(h)→0\rho(h)\to 0.

For the fixed-coefficient construction, let 𝟏B​(a)\mathbf{1}_{B}(a) be the indicator of membership in BB, and set cρ​(h)=β−1​log⁡(m⁡(1−ρ⁡(h))/((1−m)​ρ​(h)))c_{\rho}(h)=\beta^{-1}\log\!\bigl(m(1-\rho(h))/((1-m)\rho(h))\bigr). Starting from a zero score, introduce the error eρ​(h,a)=cρ​(h)​(𝟏B​(a)−ρ⁡(h))e_{\rho}(h,a)=c_{\rho}(h)(\mathbf{1}_{B}(a)-\rho(h)). This error is centered, and

𝔼a∼qS+(⋅∣h)[eρ(h,a)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)}[e_{\rho}(h,a)^{2}] (18)
=ρ​(h)​(1−ρ​(h))β2​(log⁡m⁡(1−ρ⁡(h))(1−m)​ρ​(h))2→0.\displaystyle=\frac{\rho(h)(1-\rho(h))}{\beta^{2}}\left(\log\frac{m(1-\rho(h))}{(1-m)\rho(h)}\right)^{2}\to 0.

The score difference between BB and its complement is cρ​(h)c_{\rho}(h). Therefore,

qβ​(B∣h)=ρ⁡(h)​eβ​cρ​(h)1−ρ⁡(h)+ρ⁡(h)​eβ​cρ​(h)=m.q_{\beta}(B\mid h)=\frac{\rho(h)e^{\beta c_{\rho}(h)}}{1-\rho(h)+\rho(h)e^{\beta c_{\rho}(h)}}=m. (19)

This establishes the contrast. □\square

Adaptation to score scale.

For an extrapolation coefficient β≥0\beta\geq 0, consider the normalized target q~β​(a∣h)∝qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[β​dη​(h,a)]\tilde{q}_{\beta}(a\mid h)\propto q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp[\beta d_{\eta}(h,a)]. For a scale factor c>0c>0, if the constraint binds, replacing dη​(h,a)d_{\eta}(h,a) by c​dη​(h,a)cd_{\eta}(h,a) leaves the boundary target unchanged whenever the coefficient cap permits reaching it. The selected coefficient becomes β/c\beta/c, and

qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[βc​c​dη​(h,a)]\displaystyle q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp\!\left[\frac{\beta}{c}\,cd_{\eta}(h,a)\right] (20)
=qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[β​dη​(h,a)].\displaystyle=q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp[\beta d_{\eta}(h,a)].

Thus, at active prefixes, a positive rescaling of the direction changes the selected coefficient but not the target.

Connection to response length.

ExOPD reports increasing response length under stronger extrapolation and identifies amplification of biased log-ratios as a possible source of instability (Yang et al., 2026). The fixed-coefficient counterexample above describes one mechanism that could contribute to this behavior. If teacher-rare tokens that prolong or repeat reasoning receive spuriously large scores, fixed-strength extrapolation can assign them substantial probability. Our KL constraint limits this amplification at each prefix.

H.2 Direction

Proof of Proposition 2.

Write the objective in Eq. (9) as Fh​(d​(h,⋅))F_{h}(d(h,\cdot)). Completing the square gives

Fh​(d⁡(h,⋅))−Fh​(dη​(h,⋅))\displaystyle F_{h}(d(h,\cdot))-F_{h}(d_{\eta}(h,\cdot)) (21)
=(1σT2​(h)+1σπ2​(h))\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{T}^{2}(h)}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{\pi}^{2}(h)}\right)
⋅𝔼a∼qS+(⋅∣h)[(d(h,a)−dη(h,a))2].\displaystyle\cdot\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)}[(d(h,a)-d_{\eta}(h,a))^{2}].

The solution in Eq. (10) is centered, so it is feasible. The coefficient is positive, establishing uniqueness. □\square

This solution gives more weight to the nearer reference. Its direction is proportional to σπ​(h)​u​(h,a)+σT​(h)​v​(h,a)\sigma_{\pi}(h)u(h,a)+\sigma_{T}(h)v(h,a), where u⁡(h,a)=ΔTc​(h,a)/σT​(h)u(h,a)=\Delta_{T}^{c}(h,a)/\sigma_{T}(h) and v⁡(h,a)=Δπ0c​(h,a)/σπ​(h)v(h,a)=\Delta_{\pi_{0}}^{c}(h,a)/\sigma_{\pi}(h).

Conflicting signals.

If the normalized signals point in opposite directions, u⁡(h,a)=−v⁡(h,a)u(h,a)=-v(h,a) for all a∈S⁡(h)a\in S(h), their equal-weight sum vanishes. Our combination instead satisfies

dη​(h,a)=σT​(h)​σπ​(h)​(σπ​(h)−σT​(h))​u​(h,a)σT2​(h)+σπ2​(h).d_{\eta}(h,a)=\frac{\sigma_{T}(h)\sigma_{\pi}(h)(\sigma_{\pi}(h)-\sigma_{T}(h))u(h,a)}{\sigma_{T}^{2}(h)+\sigma_{\pi}^{2}(h)}. (22)

It remains nonzero when the reference distances differ and follows the signal from the nearer reference. When the reference distances are equal, the signals cancel and the target remains qS+(⋅∣h)q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h).

For example, consider a two-token support with π0(⋅∣h)=(0.1,0.9)\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid h)=(0.1,0.9), tref(⋅∣h)=(0.5,0.5)t_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid h)=(0.5,0.5), and q+(⋅∣h)=qS+(⋅∣h)=(0.3,0.7)q^{+}(\cdot\mid h)=q_{S}^{+}(\cdot\mid h)=(0.3,0.7). The teacher’s post-training shift favors the second token, while the teacher–student gap favors the first. Their normalized directions are opposite. Our combination gives dη​(h,⋅)≈(−0.16,0.07)d_{\eta}(h,\cdot)\approx(-0.16,0.07), so for an extrapolation coefficient β≥0\beta\geq 0, the target q~β​(a∣h)∝qS+​(a∣h)​exp⁡[β​dη​(h,a)]\tilde{q}_{\beta}(a\mid h)\propto q_{S}^{+}(a\mid h)\exp[\beta d_{\eta}(h,a)] moves probability toward the second token.

Suppose the desired distribution is π⋆(⋅∣h)=(0.2,0.8)\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid h)=(0.2,0.8), and assess a policy π(⋅∣h)\pi(\cdot\mid h) by −DKL(π⋆(⋅∣h)∥π(⋅∣h))-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid h)\|\pi(\cdot\mid h)). The teacher is better than the initial student: their divergences from π⋆(⋅∣h)\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid h) are approximately 0.02570.0257 and 0.04440.0444, respectively. Along the constructed direction, β≈2.38\beta\approx 2.38 gives q~β(⋅∣h)≈π⋆(⋅∣h)\tilde{q}_{\beta}(\cdot\mid h)\approx\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid h).
